en: The Sūtra on the Seal of the Noble Dharma Spoken by the Buddha; in the language of India, *Ārya-dharmamudrā-sūtra*;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. This...
Then the Buddha said to the bhikṣus, “Listen!
The bhikṣus replied: [“We shall listen.”]
“Yes, we shall receive your instructions,” they replied. The Buddha said,
“I shall explain for you the Seal of the Noble Dharma (āryadharmamudrā), the proper deportment, and the manifestation of pure conduct.”
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well," the Buddha said.
"O bhikṣus!"

Suppose there were someone who spoke of not seeking emptiness and not employing the state of non-conception, yet desired to give rise to and practice the karma of the meditative concentration of non-arrogance; such a thing has never existed.

Suppose there is a person who admires and delights in the dharma of emptiness, whose resolve is set upon non-conceptualization, and who gives rise to the most essential practice by eliminating the mind of self-importance and arrogance; for such a person, the work of meditative concentration can be achieved, and they will immediately fulfill their aspirations as they wish, perceiving everything universally.

Why is this? Because by aspiring to and delighting in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), desiring to attain the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñin*), and being free from the prideful view of self-importance, one can achieve all things through the work of wisdom (*prajñākarma*).
What is meant by the "Noble Seal of the Dharma" (*āryadharmamudrā*) for a bhikṣu?
This is the Seal of the Noble Dharma (*ārya-dharmamudrā*) which, through repeated practice, leads to the vision of ultimate purity.

Suppose a bhikṣu dwells in seclusion, whether sitting beneath a tree or in a quiet, open space; he understands that form (*rūpa*) is impermanent and perceives that form is fundamentally non-existent. Having understood impermanence, he further understands it as empty and non-substantial. All these are but states of vacuity; with no self and no desire, the mind comes to rest. Being naturally pure, he attains liberation—this is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). Yet, he has not yet attained the relinquishing of pride and arrogance; this is the vision of karma resulting from pure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Although he thus attains the concentration of pliancy and compliance, he immediately perceives the elimination of all perceptions of form, sound, and fragrance; for this reason, it is said that he has reached the state of non-perception and is called "desireless. Yet, he has not yet succeeded in eliminating his self-importance and arrogance, reaching only the pure vision of meditative absorption.

When his mental continuum abides in the concentration of gentleness and compliance, he perceives the elimination of all lust, hatred, and delusion; therefore, it is called the concentration of desirelessness. Yet, he has not yet attained the elimination of self-aggrandizement and pride, nor has he reached the pure vision of meditative absorption.
He thought to himself:
"From where do my own arising and ceasing originate?
Through contemplation, he understood and realized:

"That which is called 'self' arises from the habitual relishing and discrimination of various consciousnesses; all these karmas are brought about through causes and conditions, and it is from these causes and conditions that a conscious spirit (vijñāna) comes into being."
Again, he thought to himself:
"Are these various causes and conditions permanent, or are they impermanent?
Again, he thought to himself:
"That which is brought about by the convergence of causes and conditions—the conscious spirit—is entirely impermanent and lacks any fundamental basis.

This conscious spirit relies upon the impermanent to give rise to deluded thoughts; thus, there are the twelve links of dependent origination. All these ultimately resolve into exhaustion, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, destruction, separation, dispassion, and cessation."

One who clearly understands this knows that there is no fundamental basis; thus they attain subjugation, eliminate all arisings, and enter the practice of the Path. This leads to the removal of self-conceit, pride, and negligence, as well as the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the manifestation of pure conduct.
"This is what is called the seal of the noble Dharma (āryadharmamudrā), the karma of purity, from beginning to end, reaching the ultimate root and branch.
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Upon hearing this, all the bhikṣus were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.

This *Sūtra on the Seal of the Noble Dharma* was translated by the Yuezhi bodhisattva and śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa at Jiuquan on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of Yuankang. His disciple Zhu Fashou recorded it by pen. May this profound Dharma flow universally throughout the ten directions, and may the Great Vehicle shine eternally.
